outcome: A preprint by James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik claims a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, using an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph, in which forking cannot always be witnessed by a stable formula. The authors state the counterexample was found using ChatGPT 5.6. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification of the argument has yet surfaced.

ai.basis_quote: Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. ... This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol. Specifically, we prompted ChatGPT to construct a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture with a detailed series of prompts which took into account the many restrictions and likely restrictions such a counterexample would have to satisfy. ... The proofs of the relevant facts around the counterexample as well as some aspects of the specific setup have been written entirely by the authors, and no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript. (AI was used for proofreading, with the edits performed and evaluated manually by the authors.) ... In retrospect, it seems unlikely that this counterexample would have been found in the near term without the use of generative AI.

counterexample.object: The theory of an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph, in which forking (governed by an abstract independence relation encoding the order property of the random graph) cannot always be witnessed by a stable formula, contrary to the conjecture.
counterexample.verified_how: The authors state they independently wrote the proofs of simplicity (via the Kim-Pillay abstract-independence criterion) and of the failure of stable forking by hand; no independent third-party verification or expert digestion has yet been found.

summary: On 2026-08-31/2026-09, James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik posted arXiv:2609.00436, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture,' claiming to refute the 1996 conjecture of Hart, Kim and Pillay that every simple theory has stable forking (i.e. that forking is always witnessed by a stable formula). The counterexample is a specific simple theory (an infinite-dimensional vector space over a division ring of fractions of a quantum graph algebra of the random graph) in which the random graph's order property is encoded into the independence relation, so that no stable formula can witness all forking. Multiple independent checks corroborate this is a genuine, real preprint rather than a fabricated result: Scott Mutchnik's own academic homepage (sites.google.com/berkeley.edu/scottmutchnik) lists 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, with James Freitag (using ChatGPT 5.6), preprint' among his own works, and both authors are established, active model theorists with a real, independently verifiable 2025 co-authored paper (with John Baldwin) findable via web search. This is enough to establish the event and the AI-attribution as coming from the authors' own account, satisfying the bar for `ai_role: generated` and `status: claimed`. However, I flag real uncertainty in the secondary sourcing: several page fetches of the arXiv abstract page returned mutually inconsistent bibliographic details (a 'submitted 31 Aug 2026' notice attached to an arXiv identifier, 2609.00436, whose YYMM prefix denotes September 2026, and one listing-page fetch that did not contain the paper in an August 2026 listing but did in a September 2026 listing), and a PDF fetch returned unreadable binary content rather than text, so I could not read the manuscript's full body directly — only reconstructed abstract/section-1.1 quotes via secondary tool fetches of the abstract/HTML page, which I cross-checked against each other and against the author's own homepage listing for consistency. The model name 'ChatGPT 5.6' / 'GPT-5.6 Sol' is unfamiliar to me (my knowledge cutoff is January 2026), which is expected for a system released after cutoff but is also a reason for caution given the fetch inconsistencies above. No expert digestion (a Tao-style walkthrough, journal acceptance, or independent re-derivation by a third model theorist) has surfaced; a companion blog post (Kevin Buzzard's Xena blog, 2026-07-20) discusses a wave of similar 2026 AI-found counterexamples to other conjectures (Erdős unit distance, a Grothendieck group-scheme question, the Jacobian conjecture) with emphasis on Lean-checked verification, but does not mention this problem, so the stable forking result has not received that level of independent scrutiny. Status is therefore `claimed` rather than `resolved`: a preprint with a clear authorial account of AI involvement in constructing the counterexample, not yet digested by the field.
competing_reading: If the bibliographic inconsistencies in the fetched arXiv metadata (date vs. identifier mismatch) reflect an actual data problem rather than tool/fetch noise, there is a small chance this record is describing a paper that does not exist as described, or exists with different details than reported here. I weighed this against corroboration from Mutchnik's own institutional homepage, which independently lists the same paper with the same AI attribution, and judged the corroboration sufficient — but a reader with direct arXiv access should re-verify the raw abstract page and PDF text before treating this as fully settled.
what_would_settle_it: Direct, verified access to the raw arXiv abstract page and PDF text of 2609.00436 (rather than reconstructed tool summaries), and evidence of expert digestion or peer review — e.g. a referee report, journal acceptance, or a model theorist's independent write-up confirming the proof of simplicity and the failure of stable forking.
